title: Effacement
hook: "others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here": forty-four resolves (MN 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stained cloth, and your line, clean cloth takes dye. Did you clear one small thing before starting something good? Day four hundred eight.
screen: `THE STAINED CLOTH — CLEAN CLOTH TAKES DYE.`

segments.voice: In almost any group there comes a moment when someone says: everyone does it. Everyone pads the expense report a little. Everyone talks about the boss when she's out of the room. Everyone's a bit cruel online; it's just how it works. It's hard to argue with, mostly because it's often true, at least a little. A discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings has an answer to it, set out forty-four times. Today: effacement.
screen: `EVERYONE DOES IT.` → `HARD TO ARGUE WITH.` → `AN ANSWER, FORTY-FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: MN 8, the Sallekha. A monk named Mahacunda asks how to let go of the many views people hold about the self and the world. The Buddha's answer begins somewhere unexpected. A monk might reach the deep meditative states, the jhanas, and think he's effacing. He isn't, the Buddha says. They're pleasant abidings, peaceful abidings, here and now. Effacement is something else. Sallekha comes from a verb meaning to scrape away, to pare down: the slow whittling of what doesn't belong. And then comes the refrain. Others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here: that is how you should efface. Others will kill living beings; we won't. Others will take what isn't given; we won't. Others will speak falsely, maliciously, harshly, idly; we won't. Others will be envious, stingy, deceitful, arrogant, hard to correct; we won't. Others will cling to their own views and let them go only with difficulty; we won't. Forty-four in all. Two things stand out. The refrain doesn't condemn the others. It never adds: and they're terrible. It says: here, among us, this is how we'll be. It draws a line around your own conduct. And it doesn't wait for everyone else to agree first. The Buddha gives a picture: just as there might be an uneven road, and another, even road to go around it, so not being cruel is the even road around cruelty. And the sutta ends with a line he repeats to many students: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't delay, or you'll regret it later.
screen: `JHANAS ARE NOT EFFACEMENT.` · `SALLEKHA — PARING DOWN.` · `OTHERS WILL; WE WON'T, HERE.` · `THE EVEN ROAD AROUND.` · then, large: `OTHERS MAY, WE WON'T.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the refrain run quietly, one line per breath. Others may be harsh; I won't be harsh here. Others may gossip; I won't gossip here. Others may cling to their views; I won't cling here. Let one of them land, the one that fits your week. Then drop the words, and just sit with that one resolve, like a smooth stone in your pocket. The bell holds the time.
Sallekha. Effacement: paring away what's unhelpful, line by line, whatever others are doing.
Your line: others may, we won't. Today, when you hear everyone does it, quietly keep your one resolve anyway. Day four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers often use the Sallekha Sutta's refrain as a model for personal resolves, and monastic training emphasizes keeping one's own conduct whatever others around one do.

pairs: asks how to let go of views

fork.setup: everyone at work pads their expense reports a little. in the spirit of MN 8, what's the line?
options: everyone does it, so it's fine
fork.reveal: the refrain doesn't judge the others or wait for them. it simply says: here, we won't. that's effacement.

original.note: Pali sallekha: effacement, paring down; from a verb meaning to scrape or pare.

trapdoor: what you thought: effacement, like being shy or self-effacing.
what it means: paring away unhelpful habits, whatever the people around you do.
what a scholar hears: the sutta's closing words, roots of trees and empty huts, meditate and don't delay, recur as the Buddha's parting instruction in several discourses.

notes: The forty-four items are summarized, not listed; the order of examples in the teach is approximate.
Etymology of sallekha (to scrape, pare down) stated simply; please confirm.
The 'roots of trees, empty huts' closing appears in several suttas (e.g. MN 19, MN 106); please confirm it closes MN 8.
